issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, 'institutional failure' and especially 'betrayal by someone trusted' are hard to reconcile unless the crash involved unusual interpersonal circumstances not reflected anywhere else in the profile. The rest of the profile centers on fear/startle/intrusive sensory recall, which fits an accident trauma; these appraisal items instead imply an interpersonal or systemic-trauma narrative.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: 'Guilt on recall' can occur after accidents, but in this profile it sits awkwardly with the chosen appraisal set: the appraisals focus on betrayal/institutional failure rather than self-blame or responsibility. That makes the guilt theme insufficiently supported across nodes for a coherent cognitive formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, the appraisal 'I was betrayed by someone I trusted' is hard to reconcile unless the crash specifically involved a trusted driver or intentional wrongdoing, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere else in the profile. As presented, it introduces a different interpersonal-trauma theme that is not supported by the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'Betrayal' and 'Self-Blame' can sometimes coexist, but in this profile they point to different causal narratives for the trauma (trusted other's betrayal vs one's own actions causing the event) without any supporting context. That makes the appraisal set clinically hard to unify around a single MVC trauma narrative.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: The profile contains a hard-to-reconcile blame pattern: strong self-blame and guilt are paired with other-blame rumination as a core maladaptive strategy. Mixed blame can occur, but this combination is the main internal inconsistency in the selected items because the appraisals and memory items point toward inward blame, while the strategy item points toward sustained outward blame.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Within the cognitive formulation, Maladaptive Strategies links most strongly to Negative Appraisals, so the strategy content should fit the appraisal style. Here the appraisal style is dominated by self-blame, helplessness, and permanent emotional damage, making other-blame rumination the least coherent strategy item.

issues.item: Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, guilt on recall is plausible, especially with self-blame, so it is not problematic by itself. The concern is specifically its combination with persistent other-blame rumination, which pulls the profile toward a different blame direction than the rest of the formulation.

vignette: Alejandro Rivera was driving his sedan through a heavy rain when a delivery truck ran the red light at the intersection. The collision was a sudden, violent compression of space. He cannot reconstruct the sequence of events into a coherent account; the memory remains a jumble of physical sensations and broken fragments. When it surfaces, he hears the sharp hiss of the deployed airbag and the wet crack of his own rib cage under the dashboard. Each time those sounds return in his mind, a heavy shame settles over him, as if the wreck had been a direct reflection of his moral character. He became certain that he would never experience his former emotional landscape again, that his capacity for ordinary feeling was permanently severed. He also arrived at the quiet conviction that he was utterly powerless to prevent calamity, and that the accident had occurred precisely because of the kind of man he was. Alongside these beliefs, a current of strong negative emotions-fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame-frequently rose without warning, sharp and unbidden. In the months that followed, these beliefs and sensations coexisted with a heightened vigilance that colored his days. Alejandro began scanning for doorways and fire exits the moment he stepped into any new space. At the rehearsal studio where he taught contemporary dance, the narrow staging doors and mirrored walls became rooms he had to map before breathing easily. When his wife, Elena, or a choreographer reached out to correct his stance without warning, his body would jump with alarm, shoulders tightening, breath catching. He tried hard to push the trauma from his thoughts whenever it intruded, forcing his attention toward the metronome or the music cue. When the suppression failed, he deliberately let his awareness drift, stepping out of his body until the present felt distant and flat. He also began delaying sleep, staying awake until very late in the night, convincing himself that if he simply remained upright, he would not have to face what waited in the dark. The daily weight of these experiences accumulated in quiet, concrete ways. He stopped teaching the lifts and partner work, telling his students he was preserving his joints, though the reality was that standing near them meant risking an unexpected touch. He found himself sitting in his parked car long after the building emptied, hands resting on the wheel, eyes tracking the garage doors even though he was already outside. The distance between him and Elena grew not from arguments, but from his steady retreat into wakefulness and mental quieting. He watched his students' faces harden slightly when he canceled sessions, and he noted how his own voice had lost its usual cadence, replaced by a flat, measured tone. At sixty-two, the exhaustion of maintaining this constant separation finally outweighed his usual reserve. He noticed how the shame on recall was bleeding into his conversations with Elena, how the helplessness made even running errands feel like navigating unpredictable terrain, how the blank spaces in his memory were no longer manageable silences but persistent gaps in his own identity. He scheduled an intake because the quiet had become too heavy to carry alone. What he hoped for was not a dramatic reversal, but a chance to stop fighting his own nervous system, to feel the floor beneath his feet without flinching, and to believe, however tentatively, that he was not fundamentally broken by the night the metal gave way.
